extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, tribunal administrators, lawyers and policy analysts interested in pension/benefits appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the Pension Appeal Board's (PAB) jurisdiction, procedures, publication practices, and statistics for appeals under the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Quebec Pension Plan (QPP) and related schemes. Focuses on referral practice, powers on review, publication/digesting of decisions, recordkeeping and empirical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to the PAB under section 86(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referral process under section 86(2) — ostensibly for the Umpire to leave to the PAB determination of a particular question bearing specifically on section 3 raised in an appeal pending before him; in practice used differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice subsection (2) is often used where Minister rules simultaneously on inclusion questions for CPP and unemployment insurance; the Umpire frequently refers matters (either on his own initiative or at a party's request) to the PAB to abbreviate appeals, avoid conflict between tribunals, accelerate and consolidate appeals, and promote consistency on inclusion questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB powers on referred cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Although section 87 does not specify the PAB's powers when faced with a case referred by the Umpire, there is no reason to suppose they differ from its powers in ordinary appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PAB may substitute its own judgment for that of the Minister in all questions of law connected with interpretation and application of section 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between internal review and contentious review
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Review' as used in section 190 of the QPP is terminologically loose; internal review differs from contentious review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal review: the author of the initial decision is requested to modify his own decision. Contentious review: appeal to a distinct or higher authority asked to substitute its own decision. Within section 190 the Review Commission's 'review' corresponds to an appeal in the strict sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Commission powers under sections 191 and 192
rubrics_metrics.description: The Review Commission may 'reverse, affirm or vary' a challenged decision and 'has authority to decide any question of fact or of law'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These explicit powers indicate a full appellate authority able to substitute its decision on questions of fact or law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to appeal and time limits (QPP)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to appeal under the QPP is not subject to leave and appeals must be lodged within 90 days, a period that may be extended by the Commission Chairman upon application within the statutory time limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors federal law (CPP) practice and is likely for similar policy reasons; the Chairman has discretion to extend time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of decisions subject to appeal under section 190
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions made by the Minister of Revenue of Quebec are subject to appeal under section 190; two types distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First: decisions following a request for a ruling on an individual's obligation to pay contributions (sec. 62), raising questions dealt with by sections 1–7 of the QPP. Second: decisions arising from objections to notices of assessment (sections 65–66) — hierarchical review analogous to 'appeal to the Minister' under CPP section 28(2); these generally involve sections 1–7 or 36–52.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of final decision qualifying self-employment
rubrics_metrics.description: A final decision (by Minister or Commission) qualifying an occupation as self‑employed terminates the Commission's jurisdiction and transfers the case to fiscal authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transfer creates the risk of conflict between the Review Commission and fiscal tribunals. Unlike the CPP, the QPP contains no provision for removing such litigation from fiscal tribunals by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of QPP benefits jurisdiction (section 196)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original section 196 assigned jurisdiction over QPP benefits litigation to the Review Commission; effective August 1, 1975 this was replaced by a provision assigning jurisdiction to the Social Affairs Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The earlier designation of proceedings as 'review' was terminologically inaccurate; the replacement gave the more correct designation of 'appeal' for actions before the Social Affairs Commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of Review Commission under former section 196 (benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the original section 196 the Review Commission could 'affirm or vary' a disputed decision, authorize payment of benefits, determine amounts, or decide that no benefits were payable and 'decide any question of fact or of law'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constituted a full appeal jurisdiction in the strict sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB approach to hearings (de novo examination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB considered its hearings as de novo examinations of cases brought before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justified in QPP context because the PAB was often the first appeal tribunal and could not rely on findings of any prior appellate body; applied similarly to federal cases consistent with Jaeger decision principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on substituting judgment in discretionary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB disclaimed the right to substitute its judgment for that of the Pension Board in exercising discretionary powers conferred upon the latter (Resnick v. Quebec Pension Board).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These discretionary powers were conferred by sections 105 and 107 of the QPP (equivalent of original CPP section 63). Replacement of the Review Commission by the Social Affairs Commission later reversed caselaw on this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to exhaust internal review before appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: To be subject to appeal a decision had to be one handed down by the Pension Board following a request to re‑examine its initial decision; all available internal review mechanisms had to be exhausted as a condition of lodging an appeal and proceeding to contentious review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial unfavourable decisions by the Pension Board could not be challenged directly by appeal to the Review Commission without exhausting hierarchical/internal review first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrar's discretionary power to publish PAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Registrar may arrange for the publication of the decisions of the Board, or a digest thereof in such form and manner as the Board deems proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication of PAB decisions is a possibility, not an obligation; realization depends on Registrar initiative and Board discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of PAB decisions and Official Languages Act obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB formulates its decisions in the language used by the appellant; the Official Languages Act obliges federal administrative tribunals to deliver or publish in both official languages decisions which resolve questions of law of interest or importance to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While using the appellant's language appears satisfactory for parties, it is less so for eventual caselaw users who may be unilingual; the PAB appears to fall short of its statutory duty under the Official Languages Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of private publisher/digest and language practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Registrar forwards drafted decision texts to a Toronto publisher who produces an updated practical guide to pension plans and social benefits; the guide is published in English only and includes PAB decisions delivered in French preceded by an English synopsis produced by the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide is primarily for lawyers and business leaders, is sold with subscription updating, and contains legislation, commentary, rules of procedure, forms, directories and a (non-caselaw) index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of settlement-only decisions from the Digest
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions in which the PAB limits itself to stating the terms of a settlement effected between the parties before the hearing are excluded from the Digest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion affects which decisions become part of the published caselaw available to practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digest organisation and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgments in the Digest are collected in chronological order without distinction as to CPP/QPP or contributions/benefits; the publisher assigns a serial number distinct from the PAB's official case number (the latter not indicated in the Digest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publisher's serial number is used for reference in the table of contents and for practitioners using the Digest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequacy and inconsistency of annual report statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: CPP and QPP annual reports contain only abbreviated synopses of data (e.g., number of appeals brought and pending) and often present data differently year-to-year; figures may disagree between reports or within a report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes it difficult to obtain an accurate historical perspective or reliable view of workloads from official annual reports alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB's internal recordkeeping (Registrar's roll) initiated June 1975
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board kept no statistical record of its own activity until June 1975 when the Registrar's office began to keep a roll of hearings indicating essential elements of each appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The roll includes only cases ready for hearing (which may be months after lodgement) but has been useful for detailed analysis of PAB activities (e.g., July 1, 1975–Dec 31, 1976).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories for classifying case status in statistical tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables classify cases year-by-year with counts for: filed away following Chairman's refusal to give leave to appeal; filed away following withdrawal of appeal; settled by a PAB decision (distinguishing substantive decisions and decisions recording out-of-court settlement); still pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of classification is used across several tables (VII–XI) to describe PAB workload in distinct jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: High withdrawal rates and effect on effective workload
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantial number of appeals are withdrawn before hearing; for CPP contributions only about one-half of appeals lodged normally reach the hearing stage (estimated by applying post-1974 withdrawal rates to pending cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal rates vary by jurisdiction; withdrawal and leave-denials substantially reduce the effective workload. Also some hearings are summary where the PAB merely records settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of hearings conducted as summary procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A notable fraction of hearings are brief summary procedures where the PAB merely takes notice of prior out-of-court settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately one-fifth of hearings in CPP contributions and about one-quarter of decisions in CPP benefits are of this reduced/summary type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical concentrations of litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain regions produce more appeals relative to their population share (e.g., Nova Scotia, Northern Ontario, BC interior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concentrations correlate with industries posing higher health risks (coal, mining, logging) and with procedural factors (speed of pre-litigation stage, clarity of notification of appeal rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness metric: PAB decisions outcome rates (CPP contributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical chance of appellants having the PAB reverse challenged decisions — in CPP contributions, of 29 PAB decisions recorded in the CCH Digest (1968–1976), the PAB upheld the Minister in 23 cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields an appellants' success rate of approximately 20% (analysis based on CCH Digest and sample from Registrar's roll).
